{{family name hatnote|Shu|lang=Chinese}}
'''Shu Hongbing''' ({{zh|s=舒红兵}}; born January 1967) is a Chinese [[Cell biology|cytologist]] and [[Immunology|immunologist]]. He became a member of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] in 2011 and [[TWAS]] in 2012. Shu is mainly known for his work on cell [[signal transduction]] related to [[Immunity (medical)|immunity]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://en.whu.edu.cn/info/1073/1585.htm |title=Shu Hongbing |publisher=Wuhan University |access-date=14 September 2014}}</ref>

==Life==
Shu Hongbing was born to a poor rural family in [[Rongchang County, Chongqing]]. His mother died when he was 9 years old. When Shu entered senior high school, he failed the chemistry exam, and did not know any English.<ref name="zhonghua"/> He had to go to school barefoot because he could not afford to buy shoes.<ref name="zhonghua"/> However, by the time he finished high school with a national stipend in 1983, he was accepted by [[Lanzhou University]] with the highest [[National Higher Education Entrance Examination|National Matriculation Examination]] score in his class.<ref name="zhonghua">{{cite web |last=凤栖|url=http://elite.youth.cn/gnb/201311/t20131108_4171300.htm|title=舒红兵 从海外揽回的生命科学"少帅" |date=8 November 2013|publisher=中华儿女报刊社 |access-date=14 September 2014}}</ref> After graduating in 1987, Shu entered the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Basic Medical Institute Cell Laboratory, where he obtained his master's degree three years later.<ref name="Hubei">{{cite web|author=别鸣|url=http://hbrb.cnhubei.com/html/hbrb/20130613/hbrb2065879.html|title=舒红兵院士的生命情怀|date=13 June 2013|publisher=Hubei Daily|access-date=15 September 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140915090950/http://hbrb.cnhubei.com/html/hbrb/20130613/hbrb2065879.html|archive-date=15 September 2014}}</ref>

In 1990, Shu went to the United States and worked as a research assistant at the [[University of Michigan]] Medical Center. In 1992, he became a postgraduate student at [[Emory University]], where he earned his Ph.D. within 3 years.<ref name="zhonghua"/> In 1995, he entered [[David Goeddel]]'s laboratory at Tularik. In 1998 he became an assistant professor at the Department of Immunology of the [[National Jewish Medical and Research Center]]; he was promoted to associate professor in 2003.<ref name="Dushi">{{cite web|url=http://www.cqdsrb.com.cn/article-1211-1.html|title=舒红兵|date=27 April 2013|publisher=武汉大学病毒学国家重点实验室|access-date=5 October 2014|archive-date=6 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006111153/http://www.cqdsrb.com.cn/article-1211-1.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1999 Shu became a [[Changjiang Scholars Program|Changjiang scholar]] and part-time professor at [[Peking University]] School of Life Sciences. At the end of 2004, [[Wuhan University]] College of Life Sciences employed him as the dean. In December 2011, he was elected as a member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. In September 2013, he was appointed as a vice-president of Wuhan University.<ref>{{cite web|last=夸克|url=http://www.cqdsrb.com.cn/article-1211-1.html|title=荣昌偏远农家 走出中科院"最年轻"院士|date=20 December 2013|publisher=都市快报|access-date=18 September 2014|archive-date=24 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140924041407/http://www.cqdsrb.com.cn/article-1211-1.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>  In 2015, Dr. Shu was given a Mid-Career [http://www.nature.com/nature/awards/mentorship/ Mentoring in Science Award] by the well-known journal [[Nature (journal)|Nature]].<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.nature.com/nature/mentoringawards/china/|title = Nature awards for creative mentoring in science - China|website = www.nature.com|access-date = 2016-05-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last = Gerstner|first = Ed|date = 2015-12-16|title = Mentorship: Stewards of China's future|journal = Nature|language = en|volume = 528|issue = 7582|pages = 427–428|doi = 10.1038/nj7582-427a|pmid = 26682340|doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url = http://en.whu.edu.cn/info/1081/2095.htm|title = Professor Shu Hongbing Wins the Nature Award for Mentoring-Wuhan University|website = en.whu.edu.cn|access-date = 2016-05-26}}</ref>

==Research==
In 1999, Shu's team studied downstream signaling by [[TRAIL]] receptors. They discovered that a signaling cascade can mediate TRAIL-induced [[NF-kappaB|NF-κB]] activation, and TRAIL-induced [[apoptosis]] cannot be blocked by it.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hu WH, Johnson H, Shu HB |title=Tumor necrosis factor-related apoptosis-inducing ligand receptors signal NF-kappaB and JNK activation and apoptosis through distinct pathways |journal=J. Biol. Chem. |volume=274 |issue=43 |pages=30603–10 | date=October 1999 |pmid=10521444 |doi= 10.1074/jbc.274.43.30603|doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2000, he and his colleagues showed that [[FADD]], [[Casper (protein)|Casper]] (caspase-8-related protein), and [[caspase-8]] play important roles in NF-kappaB activation pathways.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hu WH, Johnson H, Shu HB |title=Activation of NF-kappaB by FADD, Casper, and caspase-8 |journal=J. Biol. Chem. |volume=275 |issue=15 |pages=10838–44 | date=April 2000 |pmid=10753878 |doi= 10.1074/jbc.275.15.10838|doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2002 they used [[two-hybrid screening]] to identify [[TNFRSF13C|BAFF-R]]-associated downstream proteins, showing that [[TRAF3]] can inhibit BAFF-R-mediated NF-kappaB activation and IL-10 production.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Xu LG, Shu HB |title=TNFR-associated factor-3 is associated with BAFF-R and negatively regulates BAFF-R-mediated NF-kappa B activation and IL-10 production |journal=J. Immunol. |volume=169 |issue=12 |pages=6883–9 | date=December 2002 |pmid=12471121 |doi= 10.4049/jimmunol.169.12.6883|doi-access=free }}</ref> They also cloned and identified a novel [[Apoptosis-inducing factor|AIF]]-homologous molecule called AMID, which can lead the way to [[caspase]]-independent apoptosis.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Wu M, Xu LG, Li X, Zhai Z, Shu HB |title=AMID, an apoptosis-inducing factor-homologous mitochondrion-associated protein, induces caspase-independent apoptosis |journal=J. Biol. Chem. |volume=277 |issue=28 |pages=25617–23 | date=July 2002 |pmid=11980907 |doi=10.1074/jbc.M202285200 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2005, his team identified a novel molecule that serves as a signal transfer station. Previously in 2003, a Japanese team had already demonstrated several genes involved in NF-kappaB activation. Shu's team discovered that over-expression of one of these genes had a strong effect on [[IRF3]] activation. Through a series of experiments, they discovered that the product of this gene greatly influences [[TLR3]]-independent IFN-β signaling. It was named [[Mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein|VISA]] (virus-induced signaling adaptor). It can also interact with [[TRIF]] and [[TRAF6]], and plays an essential role in virus-triggered TLR3-independent and TLR3-mediated antiviral IFN signaling.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Xu LG, Wang YY, Han KJ, Li LY, Zhai Z, Shu HB |title=VISA is an adapter protein required for virus-triggered IFN-beta signaling |journal=Mol. Cell |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=727–40 | date=September 2005 |pmid=16153868 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2005.08.014 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2008 they discovered another adaptor protein, MITA, through expression cloning. MITA is related to VISA, and has the ability to mediate virus-triggered IRF3 activation and IFN expression.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Zhong B, Yang Y, Li S, etal |title=The adaptor protein MITA links virus-sensing receptors to IRF3 transcription factor activation |journal=Immunity |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=538–50 | date=October 2008 |pmid=18818105 |doi=10.1016/j.immuni.2008.09.003 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Their later studies showed that by [[ubiquitination]] and degradation of MITA, [[E3 ubiquitin ligase]] [[RNF5]] can negatively regulate cellular antiviral signaling.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Zhong B, Zhang L, Lei C, etal |title=The ubiquitin ligase RNF5 regulates antiviral responses by mediating degradation of the adaptor protein MITA |journal=Immunity |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=397–407 | date=March 2009 |pmid=19285439 |doi=10.1016/j.immuni.2009.01.008 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In Shu's lab they also showed that SIKE, a physiological suppressor of [[IκB kinase|IKK]] epsilon and TBK1, can inhibit virus and TLR3-triggered IRF-3 activation;<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Huang J, Liu T, Xu LG, Chen D, Zhai Z, Shu HB |title=SIKE is an IKK epsilon/TBK1-associated suppressor of TLR3- and virus-triggered IRF-3 activation pathways |journal=EMBO J. |volume=24 |issue=23 |pages=4018–28 | date=December 2005 |pmid=16281057 |pmc=1356304 |doi=10.1038/sj.emboj.7600863 }}</ref> that [[RBCK1]], a ubiquitin ligase, negatively regulates TNF and IL-1 triggered inflammatory signaling;<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Tian Y, Zhang Y, Zhong B, etal |title=RBCK1 negatively regulates tumor necrosis factor- and interleukin-1-triggered NF-kappaB activation by targeting TAB2/3 for degradation |journal=J. Biol. Chem. |volume=282 |issue=23 |pages=16776–82 | date=June 2007 |pmid=17449468 |doi=10.1074/jbc.M701913200 |doi-access=free }}</ref> that DAK, a dihydroacetone kinase, can inhibit [[MDA5]];<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Diao F, Li S, Tian Y, etal |title=Negative regulation of MDA5- but not RIG-I-mediated innate antiviral signaling by the dihydroxyacetone kinase |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. |volume=104 |issue=28 |pages=11706–11 | date=July 2007 |pmid=17600090 |pmc=1913852 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0700544104 |bibcode=2007PNAS..10411706D |doi-access=free }}</ref> and that ISG56 (IFN-stimulated gene 56) is related to [[vesicular stomatitis virus|VSV]] replication, and negatively mediates virus-triggered induction of type I IFNs.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Li Y, Li C, Xue P, etal |title=ISG56 is a negative-feedback regulator of virus-triggered signaling and cellular antiviral response |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. |volume=106 |issue=19 |pages=7945–50 | date=May 2009 |pmid=19416887 |pmc=2683125 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0900818106 |bibcode=2009PNAS..106.7945L |doi-access=free }}</ref>
